summary.text: Let \(L_0=2,L_1=1\) and \(L_{n+2}=L_{n+1}-4L_n\), and set \(F_n=(2^{2n+1}L_{n+1})^2\); squaring the recurrence for \(L\) shows that \(F_{n+3}=-48F_{n+2}+3072F_{n+1}+262144F_n\). The original fourth-order recurrence yields the same relation for the odd-indexed terms, and agreement in the first three cases gives equality by induction, exhibiting the stated square root.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) be the integer sequence defined by
\[
a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=4,\qquad a_2=176,\qquad a_3=3136,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{n+4}=-4a_{n+3}+256a_{n+1}+4096a_n.
\tag{1}
\]
We prove that every odd-indexed term \(a_{2n+1}\) is a perfect square. In fact, we will give an explicit integer whose square it is.

Define an auxiliary integer sequence \((L_n)_{n\ge 0}\) by
\[
L_0=2,\qquad L_1=1,\qquad L_{n+2}=L_{n+1}-4L_n\quad(n\ge 0).
\tag{2}
\]
For each \(n\ge 0\), put
\[
w_n=2^{2n+1}L_{n+1}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
F_n=w_n^2.
\tag{3}
\]
Thus every \(F_n\) is manifestly a square of an integer. We will prove the stronger identity
\[
a_{2n+1}=F_n=\left(2^{2n+1}L_{n+1}\right)^2
\tag{4}
\]
for all \(n\ge 0\).

We first derive a recurrence involving every second term of \((a_n)\). Applying (1) with indices shifted by one and two gives
\[
a_{n+5}=-4a_{n+4}+256a_{n+2}+4096a_{n+1}
\tag{5}
\]
and
\[
a_{n+6}=-4a_{n+5}+256a_{n+3}+4096a_{n+2}.
\tag{6}
\]
Substituting (5) into (6), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{n+6}
&=-4\bigl(-4a_{n+4}+256a_{n+2}+4096a_{n+1}\bigr)
  +256a_{n+3}+4096a_{n+2}\\
&=16a_{n+4}+3072a_{n+2}+256a_{n+3}-16384a_{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
Meanwhile, multiplying (1) by \(-64\) gives
\[
-64a_{n+4}=256a_{n+3}-16384a_{n+1}-262144a_n,
\]
so
\[
256a_{n+3}-16384a_{n+1}=-64a_{n+4}+262144a_n.
\tag{8}
\]
Using (8) in (7) yields
\[
a_{n+6}=-48a_{n+4}+3072a_{n+2}+262144a_n
\qquad(n\ge 0).
\tag{9}
\]
In particular, when \(n\) is odd, this is a recurrence entirely among odd-indexed terms. If
\[
b_n=a_{2n+1},
\]
then substituting \(2n+1\) for \(n\) in (9) gives
\[
b_{n+3}=-48b_{n+2}+3072b_{n+1}+262144b_n.
\tag{10}
\]

We next show that the proposed square sequence \((F_n)\) satisfies exactly the same recurrence. The recurrence (2) gives, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
L_{n+3}=L_{n+2}-4L_{n+1}
\tag{11}
\]
and
\[
L_{n+4}=L_{n+3}-4L_{n+2}=-3L_{n+2}-4L_{n+1}.
\tag{12}
\]
We claim that
\[
L_{n+4}^2=-3L_{n+3}^2+12L_{n+2}^2+64L_{n+1}^2.
\tag{13}
\]
To verify this, write \(X=L_{n+2}\) and \(Y=L_{n+1}\). Equations (11) and (12) say that
\[
L_{n+3}=X-4Y,\qquad L_{n+4}=-3X-4Y.
\]
The right-hand side of (13) is therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
-3(X-4Y)^2+12X^2+64Y^2
&=-3(X^2-8XY+16Y^2)+12X^2+64Y^2\\
&=9X^2+24XY+16Y^2\\
&=(-3X-4Y)^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
which is precisely \(L_{n+4}^2\). This proves (13).

From the definition of \(F_n\),
\[
F_n=\left(2^{2n+1}L_{n+1}\right)^2
    =2^{4n+2}L_{n+1}^2
    =4\cdot 16^n L_{n+1}^2.
\tag{14}
\]
Using (13) and (14), we compute
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_{n+3}
&=4\cdot16^{n+3}L_{n+4}^2\\
&=4\cdot16^{n+3}
  \left(-3L_{n+3}^2+12L_{n+2}^2+64L_{n+1}^2\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
We compare the three summands with \(F_{n+2},F_{n+1},F_n\). For the first summand, removing one factor of \(16\) gives
\[
-3\cdot4\cdot16^{n+3}L_{n+3}^2
=-48\left(4\cdot16^{n+2}L_{n+3}^2\right)
=-48F_{n+2}.
\]
For the second summand, removing two factors of \(16\) gives
\[
12\cdot4\cdot16^{n+3}L_{n+2}^2
=12\cdot16^2\left(4\cdot16^{n+1}L_{n+2}^2\right)
=3072F_{n+1},
\]
because \(12\cdot16^2=12\cdot256=3072\). Finally,
\[
64\cdot4\cdot16^{n+3}L_{n+1}^2
=64\cdot16^3\left(4\cdot16^nL_{n+1}^2\right)
=262144F_n,
\]
because \(64\cdot16^3=64\cdot4096=262144\). Hence
\[
F_{n+3}=-48F_{n+2}+3072F_{n+1}+262144F_n.
\tag{15}
\]
Thus \((F_n)\) and the odd-indexed subsequence \((b_n)\) satisfy the same third-order recurrence, namely (10) and (15).

It remains to check three initial values. From (2),
\[
L_1=1,
\]
\[
L_2=L_1-4L_0=1-8=-7,
\]
and
\[
L_3=L_2-4L_1=-7-4=-11.
\]
Consequently,
\[
F_0=(2^1L_1)^2=(2\cdot1)^2=4,
\]
\[
F_1=(2^3L_2)^2=(8\cdot(-7))^2=(-56)^2=3136,
\]
and
\[
F_2=(2^5L_3)^2=(32\cdot(-11))^2=(-352)^2=123904.
\]
The first two corresponding odd terms are among the given initial values:
\[
a_1=4=F_0,
\qquad
a_3=3136=F_1.
\]
For the third, first use (1) at \(n=0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_4
&=-4a_3+256a_1+4096a_0\\
&=-4(3136)+256(4)+4096(-1)\\
&=-12544+1024-4096\\
&=-15616.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then use (1) at \(n=1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_5
&=-4a_4+256a_2+4096a_1\\
&=-4(-15616)+256(176)+4096(4)\\
&=62464+45056+16384\\
&=123904.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
a_5=123904=F_2.
\]
Equivalently, \(b_0=F_0\), \(b_1=F_1\), and \(b_2=F_2\).

We can now prove (4) by induction. The cases \(n=0,1,2\) have just been established. Suppose \(n\ge 0\) and that
\[
a_{2n+1}=F_n,\qquad
a_{2(n+1)+1}=F_{n+1},\qquad
a_{2(n+2)+1}=F_{n+2}.
\]
Applying the odd-subsequence recurrence (10) and then these induction hypotheses gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{2(n+3)+1}
&=-48a_{2(n+2)+1}+3072a_{2(n+1)+1}+262144a_{2n+1}\\
&=-48F_{n+2}+3072F_{n+1}+262144F_n\\
&=F_{n+3},
\end{aligned}
\]
where the final equality is (15). This advances the three-term induction window and proves (4) for every nonnegative integer \(n\).

Finally, by (3) and (4), for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{2n+1}=F_n=w_n^2
=\left(2^{2n+1}L_{n+1}\right)^2.
\]
Since \(2^{2n+1}L_{n+1}\) is an integer, \(a_{2n+1}\) is a perfect square for every nonnegative integer \(n\), as required.
